results.authors: Biller J, Sacco RL, Albuquerque FC, et al.
results.key_finding: Vertebral artery dissection (VAD) accounts for approximately 10-25% of strokes in patients under 45 years. Presenting features include posterior neck pain, occipital headache, dizziness, and cerebellar or brainstem infarction. Triggering factors include physical exertion, neck manipulation, and minor trauma.
results.title: Cervical Artery Dissections and Association with Cervical Manipulative Therapy: A Statement for Healthcare Professionals

results.authors: Markus HS, Hayter E, Levi C, et al.
results.key_finding: In the CADISS trial, no significant difference was found between antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapy in preventing recurrent stroke or death (2% vs 1%) in extracranial cervical artery dissection. The low recurrence rate supports either antithrombotic strategy; individualized choice based on bleeding risk and patient factors is recommended.
results.title: Antiplatelet Versus Anticoagulation for Non-cardioembolic Stroke Attributable to Cervical Artery Dissection (CADISS): Final Results

results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, Ackerson T, et al.
results.key_finding: For patients with ischemic stroke or TIA attributable to extracranial vertebral artery dissection, antithrombotic therapy for at least 3-6 months is reasonable. Mechanical thrombectomy is recommended for posterior circulation proximal vascular occlusion meeting selection criteria. Posterior fossa edema requires monitoring for decompression candidacy.
results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients with Acute Ischemic Stroke

output.summary: Vertebral artery dissection is a leading cause of posterior circulation stroke in young adults. Exertional triggers (weightlifting, sudden neck rotation) are well-documented. The CADISS trial (Lancet Neurology 2015) found no significant difference between antiplatelet and anticoagulation therapies, with overall low recurrence rates. AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines recommend antithrombotic therapy for at least 3-6 months. Posterior fossa cerebellar infarction carries risk of malignant edema requiring neurosurgical evaluation if the infarct is large. Follow-up vascular imaging at 3-6 months is indicated to assess recanalization.

Vertebral artery dissection is a leading cause of posterior circulation stroke in young adults; exertional triggers (weightlifting, neck rotation) are well-documented
T1 fat-saturated MRI of the cervical vessels is the imaging modality of choice to detect intramural hematoma (crescentic T1 hyperintensity) in vertebral artery dissection
Prodromal posterior neck pain and ipsilateral occipital headache days before stroke onset are a recognized dissection warning pattern
CADISS trial evidence supports either antiplatelet or anticoagulation for 3-6 months; individualized choice based on infarct size and bleeding risk
Cerebellar infarction with fourth ventricle compression requires serial imaging to detect malignant edema and neurosurgical readiness for decompressive craniectomy

metadata.condition_name: Acute ischemic stroke (right vertebral artery dissection)
metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate — posterior circulation stroke in a young adult with an exertional trigger. Prodromal neck pain dismissed as musculoskeletal strain is a red herring. Mild inflammatory markers and elevated LDL add confounders. The diagnosis requires recognizing posterior fossa cerebellar signs, ordering vascular imaging for dissection, and distinguishing this from SAH (thunderclap headache), vestibular neuritis, and atherosclerotic vertebrobasilar disease.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools minimum (CT, CTA, labs, MRI with fat-sat, MR_angiography or carotid_duplex), 3 red herrings (inflammatory markers, LDL, musculoskeletal anchor), requires cross-modality synthesis of DWI + T1 fat-sat + CTA findings; plausible SAH and vestibular mimics require active exclusion.
metadata.real_seed_note: Seeded from: Shi Q et al. Cerebellar infarction caused by vertebral artery dissection: A case report. Medicine (Baltimore). 2023;102(24):e33987. PMID 37327265. PMC10270511. CC-BY 4.0. Confirmed right vertebral artery dissection (V1/V3-V4 segments) with right cerebellar ischemic infarction in a 34-year-old male triggered by barbell squat exercise. Core mechanism, vessel, laterality, and exertional trigger preserved; demographics, presentation, full clinical workup, imaging, tool outputs, and ground truth are original authorship for NeuroBench v5.
metadata.revision_reason: Independent Reviewer 2 stroke audit: NCCT and CTA separated; MRI optional; CTP routed only to two extended-window cases; routine MRA/TCD/duplex duplication removed; acute labs carry explicit do-not-delay rules; EEG retained for one seizure-mimic case

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Wei Chen is a 34-year-old right-handed East Asian man with no significant medical history who presents to the emergency department via ambulance approximately 2 hours after the acute onset of severe occipital headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, right limb incoordination, and inability to walk steadily. The symptoms began abruptly during heavy barbell squat exercise at the gym, with a sharp 'thunderclap-like' posterior headache as the initiating event. He reports that over the preceding 3 days he had experienced intermittent dizziness, right-sided neck pain, and transient blurred vision, which he attributed to overexertion and a muscle strain from the gym. He dismissed these prodromal symptoms and continued exercising. Today, while completing a squat with approximately 100 kg on the barbell, he felt a sudden explosive pain at the back of his head radiating into the right side of his neck, immediately followed by severe dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and the sensation that the room was spinning. His gym partner noted that he appeared unsteady and was staggering to the right. Mr. Chen was unable to walk a straight line and was brought to the floor carefully by his training partner. An ambulance was called. He denies any loss of consciousness, facial weakness, arm or leg weakness, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, or visual field loss. He has no prior history of migraines or similar headaches. He denies any prior neck trauma, chiropractic manipulation, or recent upper respiratory tract infection. He is otherwise healthy, takes no regular prescription medications, and uses ibuprofen occasionally for gym-related neck stiffness. He denies any illicit drug use. He has never had symptoms like this before.

He had a prodromal episode of intermittent dizziness and right-sided neck pain over the preceding 3 days, which he attributed to a gym-related muscle strain.
